description: A bunch of human beings who want to know everything in detail.
summary: SOL 200 is a browser game for children aged 7 to 12 that trains them to think like a Mars astronaut, made for the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The player controls Commander Damon Carter on day 200 of the first mission to grow food on Mars, as a giant dust storm approaches the base. The player walks around a top-down pixel-art base, talks to the three other crew members, and completes short Among Us-style mini-games (checking the garden, cleaning solar panels, putting on a spacesuit, sharing limited power, restarting the oxygen machine). Each mini-game teaches one real piece of Mars science from NASA data. At key moments the player makes a two-choice decision, and every choice has a price on three meters: Safety, Mission and Team. The game teaches two things together. First, how people could survive and grow food on Mars. Second, the human side of a mission, which real astronaut training also covers: how a team decides under pressure, and how pride, fear and trust shape those decisions. The child lives these choices from inside the character: help or go alone, protect the garden or protect the crew, and learns that listening and asking for help are strengths. The facts keep the game grounded in real science, and the story keeps it from being boring. Chapter 1 is fully playable now, and the story for the remaining chapters is written, so the project can grow into a full series.
details:
Source code: https://github.com/obr7/sol200


SOL 200 turns the question "could humans live and grow food on Mars?" into a story children play, not a lesson they read. It is built with JavaScript, Canvas and Web Audio, runs in any browser on desktop and phone, and needs no account.

How it plays

  • Intro (about 78 seconds, with a Skip button). A narrated film shows the crew arguing, the launch and the arrival on Mars.
  • Explore. The player starts in the crew quarters and walks around a top-down base with 5 rooms (Crew Quarters, Control Room, Workshop, Greenhouse, Airlock) and the Mars surface. Objects with a small "?" bubble open real science cards, collected in a Discovery Journal of 13 cards. Progress is saved on the device.
  • Real NASA views. A hologram table shows a 3D Mars globe made from NASA Mars Trek maps, with 6 famous places to visit. The bedroom window shows a real Curiosity rover photo. A crew photo album tells the crew's past.
    • Garden Check: use water, a grow lamp and a heater to keep 3 plants in the healthy range; too much damages the leaves.
    • Clean the Panels: 3 jobs on 3 pairs of solar panels (brush the dust, flick off pebbles, tilt toward the Sun) before the storm hits.
    • Suit Up: a spacesuit briefing card and a card about a real Jordanian spacesuit engineer, then dress the astronaut in checklist order and do a pressure leak check.
    • Storm Night: share 6 power units between oxygen, heat, garden, lights and radio until sunrise; gusts cut the power and overloading trips the breaker.
    • Restart Rosie: reconnect the oxygen machine's wires (power, air pump, dust filter, heater) and watch CO2 become O2. If the player chose to go alone, the puzzle is harder and Marcus steps in after a failure.
  • Two decisions. Go outside or stay in during the storm. Fix the oxygen machine alone or ask Marcus for help. Every choice costs something on the Safety, Mission and Team meters, and the characters' faces show how they feel.
  • Ending. The Team meter decides the closing scene, followed by a message from Earth and a "what did you learn?" screen.

What children learn

  • Dust storms cover solar panels and cut power (Clean the Panels).
  • Power on Mars is limited, so life support comes first (Storm Night).
  • Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide, and NASA's MOXIE made oxygen from it (Restart Rosie).
  • Plants need water, light and warmth, and all three need energy (Garden Check).
  • A spacesuit is like a tiny spaceship: pressure, oxygen, heat and sealed gloves (Suit Up).
  • Solar storms send radiation to Mars, and today's real Sun changes the risk of going outside.
  • Mars geography from real maps: Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Gale and Jezero craters.
  • A sol lasts about 24 h 40 min, Mars gravity is about 38% of Earth's, and messages take minutes to reach Earth.

Real NASA data inside the game

  • Live DONKI solar flares (NASA Open APIs) set a kid-friendly Sun meter (Calm, Busy or Stormy Sun) in the mission brief, and decide how much Safety it costs to go outside. If the data cannot load, the game shows a real archived DONKI record and says so.
  • NASA Mars Trek map tiles (Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic) are loaded live to draw the 3D Mars globe on the hologram table.
  • NASA Image and Video Library: the bedroom window shows Curiosity's photo PIA20843, with its source.
  • 13 discovery cards and the mini-game cards use facts from NASA, ESA and CSA pages, each with its link.

Beyond facts: decisions, feelings and growth

  • Pressure with no perfect answer. Every option has a price, so the child feels the tension between helping and going alone, or being first and being part of a team.
  • Characters who grow. Each crew member has a fear and a past. In the full story, flashbacks at age 11 show where each fear came from, and the player's choices change how the others treat the commander.
  • Second chances. Failure never ends the game, and a later choice can repair trust.
  • Safe by design. The game does not diagnose, score or profile the child, and collects no personal data. Hard topics are shown through characters and effects, with no graphic scenes.

Chapter 1, which is playable now, introduces this with the commander's fear of not deserving to lead and its two decisions. The flashbacks and the deeper character stories belong to Chapters 2 to 6, which are written and planned.

Characters

  • Damon Carter (playable): the Commander. He fears that he does not deserve to lead.
  • Marcus Bell: the deputy commander. He fears being ignored again.
  • Diego Ramirez: the mechanical engineer. He fears conflict, so he hides behind jokes.
  • Layla Haddad: the plant scientist. She fears losing what she loves.

Design choices

  • Pixel-art, top-down view, with Stardew Valley-style dialogue and Among Us-style tasks and room lighting.
  • Time stops during dialogue and decisions, and failure never ends the game.
  • Characters come in 3 art styles the player can switch in Settings: the team's pixel art made with ChatGPT (default), and two styles drawn in code. Maps, furniture and effects are drawn in code, so the game loads fast on weak school computers.
  • Works with keyboard, mouse or touch, in full screen, with no account. Progress is saved on the device, with a "Reset the whole game" option.

Creativity and impact

Most space games for children teach facts. SOL 200 also teaches what real astronaut training covers: pressure, trust and teamwork. Chapter 1 is a complete slice of a six-chapter story, and it can help teachers and families talk about space science and about how we treat each other when things go wrong.
